mcqs.question: Why is crash consistency a real, recurring problem rather than a rare theoretical edge case?
options: Disks physically cannot write more than one block per power cycle
It only matters for file systems larger than 1TB
A single logical file operation is usually multiple physical disk writes, and crashes, panics, and forced VM terminations can interrupt between any of them
Modern CPUs guarantee that multi-block writes are always atomic
mcqs.explanation: Crashes are routine in production (panics, power loss, forced termination), and any of them can land between the several physical writes one logical operation requires. There's no CPU or disk guarantee that a multi-block update completes atomically, and the problem has nothing to do with file system size.

mcqs.question: In write-ahead logging, why does writing the change description to the journal BEFORE applying it to the real structures matter?
options: It makes the write faster because the journal is stored in RAM only
It removes the need to ever apply the change to the real structures at all
It only matters for file data, never for metadata
A crash before the journal commit leaves the file system untouched and valid; a crash after commit can always be recovered by replaying the journal — either outcome is well-defined
mcqs.explanation: The ordering guarantees a well-defined recovery in both crash timings: before commit, nothing real happened yet; after commit, replay finishes the job. The journal isn't RAM-only (it must be durable), and the real structures still need updating eventually — the journal entry doesn't replace that.

mcqs.question: ext4's default "ordered" journaling mode journals metadata but not file data. What guarantee does this still provide after a crash?
options: File data is always guaranteed to be the newest version written
Metadata stays structurally consistent, and data is guaranteed to be either fully old or fully new — never a corrupt mix — though it might be stale
No guarantees at all beyond what a non-journaling file system provides
Both data and metadata are guaranteed identical to full data journaling
mcqs.explanation: Ordered mode's guarantee is specifically about ordering: data is flushed before the metadata pointing to it commits, so you never end up with metadata pointing at garbage or half-written data — but the data itself could still be the pre-crash version if it wasn't flushed yet. That's a real, useful guarantee, distinct from data journaling's stronger one.

mcqs.question: Why does journal replay after an unclean shutdown typically finish in under a second, even on a multi-terabyte disk?
options: The journal only holds a small, recent window of in-flight transactions, so replay touches a handful of blocks rather than scanning the whole disk
Journal replay skips checking data integrity entirely
Modern SSDs make any operation, regardless of scope, complete in under a second
The journal is always empty by the time of a crash
mcqs.explanation: The journal is a small, bounded ring buffer of recent transactions, so replay is proportional to journal size, not disk size — a targeted operation, unlike a full fsck scan. It's about scope, not about skipping checks or being lucky that the journal is empty.

mcqs.question: A system using ext4's default ordered journaling mode crashes right after an application calls write() but before the page cache flushes. Is the written data guaranteed to survive?
options: Yes, because journaling guarantees all written data is always durable
No — ordered mode journals metadata, not file data; unflushed data in the page cache can be lost even though the file system recovers structurally intact
Yes, but only for files smaller than one block
No, because journaling only works for reads, not writes
mcqs.explanation: Journaling in ordered mode is a structural guarantee, not a data-durability guarantee. write() only lands data in the page cache; without an fsync(), a crash before flush can lose it even though the file system's metadata remains perfectly consistent. Journaling applies to both reads and writes and isn't limited by file size.

mcqs.question: Why does a database batch many row writes into one WAL entry and call fsync() once, rather than calling fsync() after every single write()?
options: fsync() is purely cosmetic and has no real performance cost
write() and fsync() have nearly identical latency, so batching provides no benefit
fsync() forces a durable disk write with latency roughly 100-1000x that of a page-cache-only write(), so batching amortizes that cost across many logical writes
Batching is required because fsync() can only be called once per file descriptor lifetime
mcqs.explanation: write() typically only touches the page cache (microseconds); fsync() blocks for an actual durable disk write, often milliseconds. Calling it per-row would multiply that cost by every row; batching many logical changes into one fsync() amortizes the expensive part across all of them. fsync() has no call-count limit.
